title: Wen Han's towel
source: School paper question (Wen Han's materials R, S, T, U)
pageIntro: Soak all four materials on the bench and weigh them again.
stem:
Wen Han measured the mass of four materials of the same size. He put each one into a container with the same amount of water for 10 minutes, then measured each mass again.

Which material, R, S, T or U, is most suitable for making a towel?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
R6090
S9090
T100150
U150180
hints: Fill in the missing column yourself: mass after − mass before.
A towel has to take as much water off your skin as it can. Which material absorbed the most grams of water?
key: Water absorbed = mass after − mass before. Never compare the "after" column on its own.

options.pick: R went from 60 g to 90 g, half as heavy again. That looks like a big change.
options.why: R absorbed 90 − 60 = 30 g. The pieces are the same size, so compare the grams of water absorbed, and T absorbed 50 g.
clash: Your readings: R absorbed 30 g, T absorbed 50 g.

options.pick: S is the tidy one: its mass did not change at all, so it seems to handle water well.
options.why: S absorbed 0 g, so it is waterproof. A towel must do the opposite and absorb as much water as possible.

options.pick: Work out the water absorbed for all four, then take the largest: 150 − 100 = 50 g.
options.why: T absorbed 50 g, more than any other material. A towel must absorb as much water as possible.

options.pick: U has the largest mass after soaking, 180 g, so it looks like it holds the most water.
options.why: U started at 150 g, so it only absorbed 180 − 150 = 30 g. The mass after soaking includes the material itself.
clash: Your readings: U absorbed 30 g, T absorbed 50 g.

title: A material for a raincoat
pageIntro: Four new materials of the same size, soaked the same way. Soak all four.
stem:
Four materials of the same size were soaked in the same way. Their masses before and after soaking are shown.

Which material is most suitable for making a raincoat?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
W4070
X8080
Y120200
Z150165
hints: A raincoat must keep the rain on the outside. What does that mean about the water it absorbs?
Look for the material whose mass did not change at all.
key: Waterproof shows up in the data as a gain of 0 g. It is the only reading that shows no water went in.

options.pick: W has the smallest mass of all, so it would make a light coat.
options.why: W absorbed 30 g, so rain would soak into it and reach the person wearing it. A light material is not the same as a waterproof one.

options.pick: Work out the gain for each one. Only X gained nothing, so only X is waterproof.
options.why: X was 80 g before and 80 g after, so it absorbed no water. A material that does not absorb water is waterproof, so the rain stays on the outside of the coat.

options.pick: Y took in the most water, so it seems to deal with rain better than the others.
options.why: Y absorbed 80 g, the most of the four. A coat made from Y would soak up the rain like a towel.
clash: Your readings: Y absorbed 80 g, X absorbed 0 g.

options.pick: Z only went up from 150 g to 165 g, a very small change for such a heavy piece.
options.why: Z still absorbed 15 g, so water went in. Only a gain of 0 g shows that no water was absorbed.
clash: Your readings: Z absorbed 15 g, X absorbed 0 g.

title: The heaviest one
pageIntro: One of these is much heavier than the rest to begin with. Soak all four.
stem:
Four materials of the same size were soaked in the same way. Their masses before and after soaking are shown.

Which material absorbed the most water?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
D200240
E50100
F150185
G90130
hints: Which material has the largest number in the "after" column? Is that what the question asks?
Write out after − before for all four before you choose.
key: The heaviest material after soaking is often just the one that was heaviest to begin with. Subtract first, then compare.

options.pick: D has the largest mass after soaking, 240 g, so it looks like it is holding the most water.
options.why: D started at 200 g and gained only 40 g. Most of that 240 g is the material itself.
clash: Your readings: D absorbed 40 g, E absorbed 50 g.

options.pick: F has large masses both before and after, so it seems to be in the running.
options.why: F absorbed only 35 g, the least of the four. Large masses do not mean large gains.
clash: Your readings: F absorbed 35 g, the smallest gain.

options.pick: G went from 90 g to 130 g, which looks like a clear jump.
options.why: G absorbed 40 g, which is less than E's 50 g. Judge by the grams absorbed, not by how big the jump looks.
clash: Your readings: G absorbed 40 g, E absorbed 50 g.

options.pick: Subtract for every row: D 40 g, E 50 g, F 35 g, G 40 g. The largest is E.
options.why: E absorbed 100 − 50 = 50 g, the most of the four, even though it has the smallest mass after soaking.

title: Two the same
pageIntro: Four materials of the same size again. Soak all four and work out your own gains.
stem:
Four materials of the same size were soaked in the same way. Their masses before and after soaking are shown.

Which two materials absorbed the same amount of water?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
P6095
Q100135
R80140
S120120
hints: You cannot answer this one by looking. Work out all four gains first.
One material gained nothing. Two of the others gained the same amount.
key: Two materials can absorb the same amount of water and still have very different masses. Only the subtraction tells you.

options.pick: Work out all four gains: P 35 g, Q 35 g, R 60 g, S 0 g. P and Q match.
options.why: Both absorbed 35 g, even though P ends at 95 g and Q ends at 135 g.

options.pick: Q and R end at 135 g and 140 g, which are almost the same.
options.why: Ending at a similar mass is not the same as absorbing the same amount. Q absorbed 35 g and R absorbed 60 g.
clash: Your readings: Q absorbed 35 g, R absorbed 60 g.

options.pick: R and S are the two unusual ones, so they feel like a pair.
options.why: R absorbed 60 g, the most of the four. S absorbed 0 g and is waterproof. They are opposites.
clash: Your readings: R absorbed 60 g, S absorbed 0 g.

options.pick: P and S have the smallest numbers before soaking or after soaking, so they look like a pair.
options.why: P absorbed 35 g but S absorbed nothing at all, so they are not the same.
clash: Your readings: P absorbed 35 g, S absorbed 0 g.

title: Was it a fair test?
pageIntro: Back to Wen Han's four materials. Soak them all again, then think about how the experiment was set up.
stem:
Wen Han soaked four materials, R, S, T and U, and measured each mass before and after soaking. The masses before soaking were all different.

Which of these had to be kept the same for a fair test?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
R6090
S9090
T100150
U150180
hints: Only one thing is allowed to change in a fair test. Here it is the type of material.
The masses before soaking were all different. Was that allowed, or does it spoil the test?
key: The different starting masses are fine: same-sized pieces of different materials weigh different amounts. That is exactly why you subtract.

options.text: The mass of each material before soaking
options.pick: The masses before soaking are all different, which looks unfair at first sight.
options.why: Same-sized pieces of different materials naturally have different masses, so this cannot be kept the same. It is handled by subtracting: water absorbed = after − before.
clash: Your readings: the masses before soaking were 60, 90, 100 and 150 g, all different, and the test still works.

options.text: The type of material in each container
options.pick: The question says "kept the same", and the materials are what the experiment is about.
options.why: The type of material is the one thing that must change. It is what is being tested.

options.text: The size of each piece, the amount of water, and the soaking time
options.pick: List everything else that could change how much water goes in, and keep all of it the same.
options.why: Only the type of material may change. If one piece were bigger, sat in more water or soaked for longer, a larger gain could be caused by that instead of by the material.

options.pick: It is something you can easily keep the same, so it sounds like a fair-test answer.
options.why: The colour of the container has no effect on how much water a material absorbs, so keeping it the same does nothing for the test.

title: A mop head
stem:
A mop head must absorb as much water as possible. Four materials of the same size were soaked in the same way.

Which material is most suitable for the mop head?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
A50110
B2045
C180230
D200200
key: Subtract for every material: A 60 g, B 25 g, C 50 g, D 0 g. The mop needs the largest gain.

options.pick: Work out after − before for all four: A 60 g, B 25 g, C 50 g, D 0 g.
options.why: A absorbed 60 g, the most of the four, so it takes up the most water.

options.pick: B more than doubled its mass, from 20 g to 45 g, which looks like the biggest change.
options.why: B absorbed only 25 g. The pieces are the same size, so compare grams of water absorbed, not how big the change looks.

options.pick: C has the largest mass after soaking, 230 g, so it seems to hold the most water.
options.why: C started at 180 g, so it absorbed 230 − 180 = 50 g, less than A's 60 g.

options.pick: D's mass did not change, so it seems to cope with water well.
options.why: D absorbed no water at all, so it is waterproof. A mop must do the opposite.

title: Rain boots
stem:
Rain boots must not absorb water. Four materials of the same size were soaked in the same way.

Which material is most suitable for making rain boots?
figure:
MaterialMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
P6075
Q150150
R3040
S100160
key: Only a gain of 0 g means a material does not absorb water. Any gain at all means water went in.

options.pick: P ends at only 75 g, a small mass, so it cannot be holding much water.
options.why: P absorbed 75 − 60 = 15 g. A small mass after soaking does not mean no water went in.

options.pick: Find the material whose mass did not change: Q is 150 g before and after.
options.why: Q absorbed 0 g, so it is waterproof. Boots made of Q keep the water out.

options.pick: R only went up by 10 g, which seems like almost nothing.
options.why: 10 g is still water absorbed. Only a gain of 0 g shows that a material does not absorb water.

options.pick: S took in the most water, so it seems to deal with rain best.
options.why: S absorbed 60 g, the most of the four. Boots made of S would soak up the rain.

title: Two cloths
stem:
Two cloths of the same size were soaked in the same way. Cloth X went from 40 g to 110 g. Cloth Y went from 150 g to 210 g.

Which statement is correct?
key: Work out each gain: X 70 g, Y 60 g. Different starting masses are expected and do not spoil the comparison.

options.text: Cloth Y absorbed more water, because its mass after soaking is larger.
options.pick: 210 g is the biggest number given, so Y seems to be holding the most water.
options.why: Y's 210 g includes the 150 g of cloth. It absorbed only 60 g, less than X's 70 g.

options.text: Cloth Y absorbed more water, because it was heavier to begin with.
options.pick: A heavier cloth seems like it would hold more water.
options.why: The starting mass is the cloth itself, not the water. Y absorbed 60 g, less than X's 70 g.

options.text: You cannot compare them, because the cloths started with different masses.
options.pick: The masses before soaking are different, which looks like an unfair test.
options.why: Same-sized pieces of different cloths naturally have different masses. Subtracting after − before gives the water each one absorbed, and those can be compared.

options.text: Cloth X absorbed more water: 70 g compared with 60 g.
options.pick: Subtract for each cloth: X 110 − 40 = 70 g, Y 210 − 150 = 60 g.
options.why: X absorbed 70 g and Y absorbed 60 g, so X absorbed more.
